While it is always a good idea to keep brush under control it would not have made any difference in this instance. The particular problem in Piedmont is that the houses are often very close together. articles.text: Piedmont City Council and City Staff gave a surprise proclamation at their January 21 Council Meeting, honoring Michael Szczech for his work as the City’s Finance Director and wishing him a relaxing retirement. A long-time resident of Piedmont, Szczech served as Finance Director for over seven years and worked his last day on Thursday, January 23. As Finance Director, Szczech administered the City’s fiscal operations, including budgeting, investments, financial transaction processing, record-keeping and reporting, payroll, accounts payable and accounts receivable. In recognition of his performance as Financial Director, the City Council officially declared Friday, January 24, 2025 as Michael Szczech Day. Originally from Chicago, Szczech is a 27-year resident of Piedmont and has raised two daughters in the city. Szczech’s wife Wendy joined the meeting to congratulate him, along with his daughters Emily and Molly joining remotely. “It’s been a great seven-and-ahalf years. I’ve worked with one of the best teams ever,” said Szczech, who described his coworkers as “the most conscientious group of employees I’ve ever worked with.” Szczech was recruited to apply for the role of Finance Director by former Mayor Bob McBain. “He far exceeded any of my expectations,” commented McBain. “He’s one of the finest professionals I’ve ever worked with, and he’s a great Finance Michael Szczech Director and a very high quality person of character and integrity.” A slew of congratulations were given by Szczech’s daughters Emily and Molly, Budget Advisory Committee Chair Frank Ryan, and every member of the City Council. Szczech is leaving big shoes to fill. The City currently is recruiting for a permanent replacement. To serve during the transition, the city council voted on November 18, 2024 to appoint Lisa Malek-Zadeh as Interim Finance Director. Malek-Zadeh will take over as Finance Director on an interim and temporary basis while the city decides on a permanent appointment. In a conversation with Szczech, the Post asked about his decision to retire. How much of a change will retirement be for you? “It will be a big change as I have been working for 52 years. It’s time to relax and find my beach!” Will you miss the short morning walk to work? “I will continue my morning walk, except I will now be accompanied by my hound dogs.” What will you miss most about working at City Hall? “I will miss the people. It is the best group of people I have ever worked with.” Do you have any advice for Piedmont’s next Finance Director? “Keep a close eye on Pension liabilities and Infrastructure needs. Make sure you dive into the details.” City Attorney Deepa Sharma (left), City Administrator Rosanna Bayon Moore, Vice Mayor Conna McCarthy, former Mayor Bob McBain, Mayor Betsy Smegal Andersen, Finance Director Michael Szczech, Wendy Szczech, Council Member Jennifer Long, Council Member Lorrell Plimier, Council Member Tom Ramsey, and Budget Advisory Committee Chair Frank Ryan Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The Piedmont Park Commission has begun a project to replace playground equipment at the Linda Beach Tot Lot. City staff presented an update at the January 14 Park Commission meeting with details of the project. The work will include replacing aging playground equipment as well as adding ADA access from Linda Avenue to the playground. The Tot Lot is currently surfaced with sand, which will be replaced with either ADA compliant matting or turf in order to install a new water fountain or bottle filling station. Funding for the project was included in the current city budget and includes a $100,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The Park Commission looked into measures to create shade at the playground as well, but were unable to find a solution within the project’s current budget. “With this generous but tight budget we just couldn’t find appropriate equipment and shade structures – either incorporated with the equipment or independent of the equipment are almost double our budget right now,” said Nancy Kent. In preparation for the project, the city’s staff will gather community input at the Tot Lot on January 30 and February 1 from 10 a.m.-12 p.m., asking questions to gauge the most important pieces of playground equipment. The City will ask attendees to share their thoughts on topics like: • What they like most about coming to the Tot Lot • Which types of equipment are most important • Balance of active versus quiet play • Choice of playground surface (samples of options will be available) For tot lot users who are unable to attend either event, an online feedback opportunity will be available next week. articles.text: After it rains, sometimes we get the chance to see a rainbow in the sky. But what causes a rainbow to form? Rainbows are created when sunlight is refracted by water droplets in the sky, resulting in a colorful display for us to observe. Did you know that this phenomenon can also be seen at night? However, instead of a rainbow, it is known as a moonbow. What causes a Moonbow? A moonbow is produced by the same process that forms a rainbow, with the Moon acting as the light source instead of the Sun. Earlier this year, observers were able to witness a moonbow in Oakland. When the right conditions align, it is a stellar sight to witness. However, such sightings are rare. Why is a Moonbow rare? Moonlight is significantly fainter than sunlight, which is why the circumstances in which you can see a moonbow, especially one with color are so rare. For a moonbow to appear, specific conditions must be met: a full or nearly full Moon, light rain, or sufficient moisture in the atmosphere to refract light, and clear skies to allow the Moon’s light to shine through. What if the moon is not completely full? A moonbow may still appear, but instead of displaying the typical colors we are familiar with, the moonbow will appear white or grey. While rainbows color our daytime sky, moonbows bring magic to our nighttime sky. They show us that even simple things like sunlight, moonlight, and raindrops can create something truly spectacular. Isabel Lopez is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a nonprofit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.

articles.text: Rob James has been named a Distinguished Eagle Scout upon nomination by the Piedmont Council and Scouting America. The award is granted to Eagle Scouts who, after over 25 years, have distinguished themselves in their life work and have voluntarily shared their talents with their communities. Rare as Eagle Scouts are, Distinguished Eagles are even rarer still, with an inaugural class dating back to 1921. Recipients include President Gerald Ford, Senators Bill Bradley and Sam Nunn, Secretary of State Rex Tillerson, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense Robert Gates, admiral Elmo Zumwalt, Astronaut Commanders Neil Armstrong (Apollo 11) and Jim Lovell (Apollo 13), film director Steven Spielberg, and Justice Stephen Breyer. Rob James has distinguished himself through his legal career and through continued service to others by following the principles of the Scout Oath and Scout Law. Now a partner with the international law firm of Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, Rob began practicing law with them in 1983. He specializes in energy, construction and infrastructure projects. He was recognized as one of the Top 100 Lawyers in California (SF and LA Daily Journal, 2006) for his work on the Chevron-Unocal merger, which thanks to an unsuccessful competing takeover bid by the Chinese National Offshore Oil Company (CNOOC) was termed by Fortune magazine as the “most politicized takeover battle in American business history.” Rob was counsel to the largest sponsor on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, with extensive travel to Russia and Kazakhstan from 1993 to 2000. “Rob was my anchor in this ground-breaking project,” wrote Michael Waller, the lead lawyer for the largest Russian company. “He was the one who I cornered, always outside the limelight, to explore the possible and chart courses to avoid the catastrophic. This transaction could have run off the rails countless times without Rob’s steady hand at the wheel. “Balancing all of the competing concerns in a multinational, multi-faceted transaction such as ours was no easy task. You have precious few opportunities to observe in real time a counterpart walk through such circumstances with such grace and dignity. Working alongside Rob James was one of those precious few opportunities for me.” Rob’s other projects as counsel have included the design and Rob’s most significant contribution is his work on Artificial Intelligence in Renewable Energy, combining two of the most transformative currents of our time. (https://www.pillsburylaw. com/images/content/1/7/178431/ AI-in-RE.pdf). He is the energy lead for the Artificial Intelligence Trust Foundation. Not surprisingly, Rob also has a deep history of pro-bono legal work, and other volunteer activities. In the field of climate change, he is Senior Research Fellow of the Institute for Responsible Carbon Removal and founding counsel of the California Resilience Challenge. He was a San Francisco Bar Association Volunteer of the Month in October 1989 for his pro bono legal services after the Loma Prieta earthquake. He contributed to legal planning for relief efforts following hurricane and superstorm damage on the Atlantic Coast and the Gulf of Mexico in the 2010s. For seven years he served in a variety of roles, including chairman of the board for the Easter Seal Society of San Francisco Bay Area. During his tenure, Rob served children and adults with disabilities through administering direct service provider programs and led fundraising campaigns for research and development of assistive devices for the disabled. Rob has also served in a remarkable array of positions as a Scouting volunteer. He earned his Eagle Scout rank in 1975 in Salinas, California. Starting in 2008, he returned to Scouting as a parent in Piedmont, serving as den leader, assistant scoutmaster, and eventually as president of the Piedmont Scout Council. He continues to serve as the Leadership and Governance lead for the territory serving all of California and Nevada. National Executive Board members Wes Smith and Anne-Marie Lamarche of Piedmont supported the local council’s nomination of Rob. “We have worked closely with Rob at the Council, Area and Territory levels and have found him to be an admirable Scouting Leader… Rob elevates every organization he touches. We believe Rob James exemplifies the DESA award through his accomplishments, impact and service to the Scouting community, as well as the high moral standard to which he holds himself and others,” they wrote. Bob Coleman, Piedmont’s most recent Distinguished Eagle, said, “It is thrilling to add Rob’s name to the list of Piedmont DESA’s. His resume adds great luster to our group.” “In addition to his skill as a leader, Rob also brings thoughtfulness, humor, and humility,” added Piedmont Council Scout Executive Kate Benson. “His willingness to serve has had a wonderful positive impact on our community.” The National Eagle Scout Association Committee, as part of Alumni Relations at the Scouting America’s national office, selected 18 recipients from throughout the U.S. this year. Members of the selection committee are all recipients of the Distinguished Eagle Scout Award. Scouting America, chartered originally as Boy Scouts of America in 1910, is the nation’s foremost youth program of character development and values-based leadership training. The Piedmont Council Scouting America runs programs within the footprint of Piedmont. Programs include Cub Scouts (youth k-5th grade), Scouts BSA (youth 11-18 years old), Venturing (youth 14-20 years old), and Exploring (career based, for youth 14-20 years old). About 1 in 4 Piedmont youth are in scouting programs, and girls are a third of the council’s membership. The character, fitness, leadership and adventure of Scouting America here in Piedmont are open to all youth. To learn more, visit www. piedmontbsa.org, or reach out to contact@piedmontbsa.org. Now a partner with the international law firm of Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman, Rob began practicing law with them in 1983. He specializes in energy, construction and infrastructure projects. He was recognized as one of the Top 100 Lawyers in California (SF and LA Daily Journal, 2006) for his work on the Chevron-Unocal merger, which thanks to an unsuccessful competing takeover bid by the Chinese National Offshore Oil Company (CNOOC) was termed by Fortune magazine as the “most politicized takeover battle in American business history.” Rob was counsel to the largest sponsor on the Caspian Pipeline Consortium, with extensive travel to Russia and Kazakhstan from 1993 to 2000. “Rob was my anchor in this ground-breaking project,” wrote Michael Waller, the lead lawyer for the largest Russian company. “He was the one who I cornered, always outside the limelight, to explore the possible and chart courses to avoid the catastrophic. This transaction could have run off the rails countless times without Rob’s steady hand at the wheel. “Balancing all of the competing concerns in a multinational, multi-faceted transaction such as ours was no easy task. You have precious few opportunities to observe in real time a counterpart walk through such circumstances with such grace and dignity. Working alongside Rob James was one of those precious few opportunities for me.” Rob’s other projects as counsel have included the design and Rob’s most significant contribution is his work on Artificial Intelligence in Renewable Energy, combining two of the most transformative currents of our time. (https://www.pillsburylaw. com/images/content/1/7/178431/ AI-in-RE.pdf). He is the energy lead for the Artificial Intelligence Trust Foundation. He was a San Francisco Bar Association Volunteer of the Month in October 1989 for his pro bono legal services after the Loma Prieta earthquake. He contributed to legal planning for relief efforts following hurricane and superstorm damage on the Atlantic Coast and the Gulf of Mexico in the 2010s. For seven years he served in a variety of roles, including chairman of the board for the Easter Seal Society of San Francisco Bay Area. Rob has also served in a remarkable array of positions as a Scouting volunteer. He earned his Eagle Scout rank in 1975 in Salinas, California. Starting in 2008, he returned to Scouting as a parent in Piedmont, serving as den leader, assistant scoutmaster, and eventually as president of the Piedmont Scout Council. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. 2. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, free compostable bags are available at City Hall to place with your green cart on garbage day. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team walked out of the last week with two wins out of its last three games. Although the Highlanders lost 74-60 to Western Alameda County Conference foes Alameda on Thursday, January 23 at Binks Rawlings Gym, they followed up with a dominant road win over Novato 66-35 two days later and had a high-score 91-44 display over Capuchino at home on Monday, January 27. The batch results bring Piedmont’s record to 11-9 with six games left in the regular season. The win over Capuchino came against a Division 4 school of the Central Coast Section, making PHS 4-0 against other D4 schools. Piedmont got all of its players on the score sheet in their 91-point drubbing of Capuchino, including double-digit points by five different players. “This is what you want for team morale late in the season. To see your starters cheering on guys just for team spirit feels pretty good. I thought our on-ball defense was aggressive and any time you can score 91 points is an accomplishment. It’s another D4 win and we could end up as high as D2 with the new NCS seeding system. When we can beat another D4 team by 40, it shows the quality of our team,” Spencer said following Monday’s win. It was a strong group of games by senior leader Ravi Silverberg, who scored 15 against Alameda, 27 vs. Novato, and 22 against Capuchino. “I’m just trusting the game plan and my teammates. My coaches are putting me in great positions. I just go out there and try to do my job. It’s a test, we have hard league games coming up, so we have to get ready for those,” Silverberg said. 74-60 loss to Alameda Alameda came out hot in the first quarter up 25-7 but Piedmont played them tight in the remaining three quarters. The Hornets held a 39-22 point lead at halftime, extending the gap to 57-38 in the third. Piedmont scored 19 points in the fourth but conceded 20. Final scorers: Silverberg and Lucian Fang-Ring scored 15 points. Dillon Casey scored 13 points, P.J. Brayer had 10, and Cash Panico scored seven. 66-35 rout of Novato Piedmont held Novato to under 11 points in each quarter, including limiting them to eight points in the second and six points in the fourth. PHS outscored them 22-10 in the first quarter and added 17 more in the second to lead 39-18 by halftime. The Highlanders scored 15 more in the third and 12 in the fourth quarter. Final scorers: Silverberg led with 27 points, Casey scored 14, Brayer had 13, while Beach Lorin and Fang-Ring had six each. 91-44 blowout win vs. Capuchino Piedmont scored over 20 points in all four quarters, but played to a tight 20-13 first quarter. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team suffered a heartbreaking 2-1 loss to Alameda on Wednesday, January 22, after conceding the game-winning goal in second-half stoppage time with less than one minute to play. Piedmont opened with a goal in the 15th minute, but struggled to find fluidity in the remaining 65 minutes of action. “It was tough. Alameda is obviously delighted with that result. It probably should’ve been a draw,” said Piedmont coach Dan Chubbock. “They managed to get that final chance and it fell to their best player who hit the shot. We just look beat up and bruised, but we have a strong enough squad where we should be able to get this game under control. We weren’t good enough tonight, simple as that.” The result brings Piedmont’s record to 4-2-6 (W-T-L) and 1-1-3 against Western Alameda County Conference opponents. To qualify for North Coast Section, PHS must finish with a .500 winning percentage on its overall record, league record, or record against fellow Division 4 schools. PHS has now lost three matches in a row, including two one-goal losses to Alameda after falling 4-3 on January 17. Piedmont was playing considerably well before winter break, including 2-1 wins over D4 school Cardinal Newman and Cal High of D1, while they went toe-to-toe with defending D1 state champions Archbishop Mitty in a 2-1 loss. Piedmont was notably without its leading scorer Elsa Wallway. Its back line has suffered considerable injuries. “We had those ups and downs last year, like how we lost to Encinal. It’s a little different now; playing Alameda so close together with the same injuries made things tough. I’d love to see how we compete when we’re at full strength,” Chubbock said. With six matches left in the regular season, the Highlanders still have an opportunity to turn things around and re-find its form. Match Recap After back and forth action to open the game, Piedmont broke through in the 15th minute when Elia Kwong broke through the defense to whip a hard shot on target. Kwong’s shot was saved and rebounded perfectly to Ryo Woltag at the left post, tapping it into the empty net. From there, both teams traded possession without anything overtly challenging. Samantha Ronen had a shot blocked in front of net in the 31st minute and had another shot trickle wide five minutes later. Alameda scored on its first good look of the game in stoppage time of the first half at 40+1 when the Hornets’ right winger sent a low cross to her forward in front of the net—slotting in the goal. Louisa Symkowick had a shot go wide at 40+3 before halftime. Piedmont struggled to create in the second half with a lot of empty long passes. Hannah Sullivan had a shot blocked in the 47th, while Woltag also had an attempt blocked in the 52nd. Sullivan had one more look in a good position in the 65th when Kyla Williams sent a cross that deflected to Sullivan, but she couldn’t make square contact on the volley attempt. The Highlanders drew just one corner in the second half in the 72nd minute, but couldn’t take advantage. Alameda’s game-winner came with around 30 seconds left in second-half stoppage time Staff Photos Ryo Woltag perfectly positioned for her goal into Alameda’s empty net. Elia Kwong pictured here taking her shot attempt which led to Ryo Woltag’s goal.

Blackwell, PHS Class of 2023, was a member of Piedmont’s Division 4 North Coast Section title and Western Alameda County Conference title-winning team in 2023. She transferred to Piedmont for her senior year after spending two years at Santiago High in Corona in Southern California and her freshman year at St. Mary’s in Stockton. She’s now a sophomore at Laney College where she has played both years. This season, Blackwell has appeared in 20 games, scoring 118 points by converting 32.8 percent from the field and 30.8 percent for 3-pointers. She has also recorded 76 rebounds, 24 assists, 10 steals, and one block. articles.text: We return to one of our earlier Hiking With Jon ventures from 2021, where you can find groves of first- and second-generation old growth redwood trees in Portola State Park. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Portola Redwoods State Park is a 2,800 acre forest, offering a shaded tour through coastal redwoods which are staggeringly larger than those found here in the East Bay. The park has 18 miles of hiking trails. Among Portola’s crown jewels is the Old Tree, an estimated 1,200 year old giant at the end of the trail that bares its name: the Old Tree Trail, an easy 1.2 mile out-and-back walk. The Old Tree is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter with burn marks still present on the bark, similar to many other trees found within Portola Redwoods. Aside The path becomes narrow on the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail. You’ll walk along Peter’s Creek on your way back to the car. A downed redwood tree at Portola Redwoods State Park. The Old Big Tree at the end of the Old Tree Trail is estimated to be 1,200 years old. The redwood is 280 feet tall and 12 feet in diameter. from the awe striking size, the thousand year old tree is among the few old growths to make it through the mass lumbering of the 1800s. Continuing back to the paved Portola State Park Road, the Summit Trail provides some uphill ascent through the hill sides for near two-miles and gaining 550 feet in elevation until intersecting with the Slate Creek Trail—turning left to start your loop back to your car, intersecting with Peter’s Creek. Turning right starts a 1.5 mile hike to a historic lumber yard, the Page Mill Site, with the Slate Creek Trail going another two miles and jolting 500 feet in elevation until its end. Portions of the Summit Trail and Slate Creek Trail narrow to less than 6-feet wide, so you’ll have to be patient when crossing other hikers. articles.text: Celebrated actor, director and filmmaker Robert Townsend takes audiences on a one-man rollercoaster ride through show business in Living the Shuffle, performing now through February 2 at The Marsh in Berkeley. The Marsh Berkeley presents the return of Living the Shuffle, a captivating one-man show by renowned actor and director Robert Townsend, being performed through February 2. Written, performed and directed by Townsend and produced by both Don Reed and Townsend, this rollercoaster of a play takes audiences through the highs and lows of show business, as Townsend shares his trailblazing career. From navigating the dangerous streets of Chicago to performing Julius Caesar at a gangster convention in New York City, Townsend chronicles his path to creating the groundbreaking film Hollywood Shuffle (1987), which launched his career and established him as a pioneer in Black cinema. In the movie, aspiring actor and hot dog stand employee Bobby Taylor (played by Townsend) catches the ire of his grandmother (Helen Martin) for auditioning for a role in the regrettably titled exploitation film Jivetime Jimmy’s Revenge. When production company Tinseltown Studios casts Taylor in the title role, he has a series of conflicted dreams satirizing African-American stereotypes in Hollywood, and must reconcile his career goals with his desire to remain a positive role model for his little brother (Craigus R Johnson). When Living the Shuffle first debuted at The Marsh Berkeley in 2019, it received rave reviews from critics and audiences alike. Theatrius wrote: “Townsend expertly weaves deeply personal moments with laugh out loud comedy,” asserting that it was “an experience unlike any [they’ve] seen before.” BroadwayWorld applauded it as “Fascinating and inspirational, 90 minutes of captivating tales and good humor.” Nicknamed one of the “godfathers of the independent film world,” Townsend is an actor, director, writer and filmmaker with over 30 years in show business and a recurring role on the FX/Hulu Emmy Winning juggernaut dramedy The Bear. Noticing the difficulty Black actors had finding jobs and the lack of consistent work available in the film industry led Townsend to create opportunities for himself and fellow artists. He co-wrote, directed, produced and starred in his first film, financed by his personal credit cards and a miracle—the critically acclaimed Hollywood Shuff le, a satire depicting the trials and tribulations of Black actors in Hollywood. Nominated for 30 NAACP Image Awards, Townsend’s prolific television work has been seen on Disney, Fox, NBC, MGM, HBO, WB and MTV. Reed, the play’s co-producer, was the 2016 Theatre Bay Area winner for Outstanding Solo Production for East 14th, and has earned recognition from the San Francisco Bay Area Theatre Critics Circle, as well as three nominations from the NAACP for Best Actor and Best Playwright. Tickets ($40 regular, $50-$100 VIP) and showtimes for performances at The Marsh Berkeley (2120 Allston Way) are available online at themarsh.org, or by phone at 415-282-3055.

articles.text: SF Ballet’s 92nd Opening Gala brings magic, glamour to New Year San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s Symphony in C choreography by George Balanchine Tamara Rojo, the artistic director of the San Francisco Ballet, may have been right in her on-stage remarks at the Company’s 2025 opening night gala at the War Memorial House this past Wednesday. From the spectacular 90-minute performance by some of the world’s finest dancers to the audience’s chance to take the floor during the after-party at the transformed City Hall, the Gala was a marvel of a celebration, one that made you proud to live in a city like ours. Say what you will about San Francisco, but there’s still plenty of art, style and revelry. The combination was particularly intoxicating on January 24th, as it all came together at the city’s Civic Center. SF Ballet’s biggest fundraising event of the year that serves as a major source of financial support for the company’s artistic and educational initiatives, the opening night gala is both an introduction to the Company’s upcoming season and an opportunity to thank patrons with exclusive performances available only that evening. As in previous years, the Gala began with a red-carpet reception and dinner at City Hall, where tables sold well in advance. The event, regularly profiled in the Town and Country magazine, drew San Francisco’s elite, including politicians, former and current mayors, banking executives, philanthropists, fashion designers, and other notable figures. This year’s honorary chair was Ayesha Curry, wife of San Francisco Warriors basketball star Stephen Curry. For the rest of the public, the doors of the War Memorial Theatre opened at 7 pm, and the foyer quickly filled with festively dressed ballet enthusiasts, laughing, chatting, and toasting. A black-tie affair, the SF Ballet’s Gala is undoubtedly the most fashionable event in town. The theatre’s marble-and-gold foyer, adorned with a dramatic red gauze canopy for the occasion, made for a natural runway. Colorful trains of elegant gowns trailed gracefully up the stairs, sparkling necklines glistened under the chandeliers, and the rhythmic click of stilettos echoed across the space. Hats, feather trims, and even the occasional (gasp) furs also made their appearance. Men’s fashion centered on classic tuxedos, though there were bold exceptions—after all, who says pumps and tutu-inspired dresses are just for women? Most importantly, everyone seemed to be enjoying themselves. Even the ushers looked pleased. At around 8 p.m. the performance chimes rang for the third time, summoning people into the auditorium. The national anthem, performed by the San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under the baton of music director and principal conductor Martin West, added a note of gravitas to the evening. It was followed by the intense and inspiring pre-curtain video short for Rojo’s third year as artistic director, whose tagline, “Transcend the ordinary!” felt right on point. Then came the first dance number: a bedroom pas de deux from Act I of Manon by Sir Kenneth MacMillan, marking its San Francisco premiere. Danced brilliantly by the SF Ballet’s rising star Jasmine Jimison and Max Cauthorn, it was a perfect foray into the company’s new season (Manon opens this Friday, January 27th). Before the next number, a vibrant Hungarian Dance from Raymonda choreographed by Tamara Rojo after Marius Petipa, honorary gala chair Ayesha Curry addressed the audience. A businesswoman, chef, author and actress, Ms. Curry is also an eloquent advocate for the art of ballet. “These dancers are top of the top of the top athletes. What they do with their bodies is unmatched,” Curry, radiant in her glittery strapless black gown said as she stood alongside Tamara Rojo, also stunning in a fitted black-and-gold tunic. “Ballet,” Curry continued, “gives you a safe space to be creative, to imagine…. I’m excited to be able to feel something tonight.” Judging by the frequent cries of “bravo” ringing through the auditorium, there was no shortage of emotion. The Three Preludes (choreographed by Ben Stevenson) perfectly illustrated Curry’s remarks about the athleticism of ballet. Classical ballet is Jasmine Jimison and Max Cauthorn in the bedroom pas de deux from MacMillan’s Manon challenging on its own, but performing on top of a ballet barre, as lead ballerina Frances Chung did in part of the piece, takes it to another level. Chung was in excellent hands with Harrison James as her partner, whose performance was flawless. Their minimalist costumes, paired with Rachmaninoff’s piano score, kept the focus squarely on the precision and beauty of their movements. Following this, Esteban Hernández, dressed in black, delivered a dramatic solo from 5 Tangos by Hans van Manen—a predictable crowd-pleaser that did not disappoint. articles.text: Acclaimed pianist Malcolm Martineau joins at Zellerbach Hall Cal Performances presents soprano singer Lise Davidsen in recital with pianist Malcolm Martineau this Tuesday, February 4, at Zellerbach Hall. Norwegian soprano Lise Davidsen will make her nationally anticipated Bay Area debut on Tuesday, February 4 at 7:30 p.m. at Zellerbach Hall on the UC Berkeley campus. She will be joined by one of the world’s most renowned collaborators on piano, Malcolm Martineau, who appeared at Cal Performances last season with soprano Erin Morley. It takes a lot to stir up the New York City classical music world, where an endless stream of virtuosic artists passes through on a weekly basis, performing in some of the world’s most iconic halls. articles.text: Winter Wandering Festival in SF Jan. 31- Feb. 2 This Friday through Sunday, join the Left Coast Chamber Ensemble for its Winter Wandering Festival, a weekend musical adventure. The festival will feature performances of “Schubert Quintet: Hay que caminar,” “On the Threshold of Dreamland,” “A Dark Matter” and “Winter Journey.” “Schubert Quintet: Hay que caminar” strikes a meaningful balance between beginning and ending, life and death. Left Coast violinists Anna Presler and Liana Bérubé will take on Italian avantgarde composer Luigi Nono’s late work “Hay que caminar… soñando” (“One must walk dreaming”), a piece defined equally by its being written in the final years of Nono’s life and at the height of his political activism. The piece is simultaneously dark and light, beautiful and uneasy — a glimpse into the mind of a composer unsatisfied with the world he is soon to leave behind. Featured side by side with the Nono masterwork is Franz Schubert’s String Quintet in C Major, a piece often cited as Schubert’s greatest achievement in all of his chamber music. It is an honest reflection on the human experience written in the final months of Schubert’s life; its iconic melodies give just as much voice to joy as sorrow, in which the end of a life sounds less like death than it does transcendence. “On the Threshold of Dreamland” combines the efforts of Left Coast and renowned Bay Area chamber choir Volti SF. World premieres by American composers Todd Kitchen and LJ White — alongside works by Laurie San Martin, Huang Ruo and Benjamin Britten — make for an eclectic, beautiful, and sometimes unsettling sonic journey. This performance will be preceded by a pre-concert talk by LJ White in Berkeley and by Todd Kitchen in San Francisco. “A Dark Matter” is sure to leave listeners refreshed as they continue on their journey. This program includes the world premiere of an eponymous piece by Bay Area composer Addie Camsuzou, and a performance of composer Gilad Cohen’s winning piece from Left Coast’s 2023 Composition Contest. “ Wi nt e r Jou r ney,” a n unabridged performance of Franz Schubert’s iconic “Winterreise,” invites listeners to think deeply about the journey they’ve undertaken. Guest tenor Kyle Stegall notes that the central figure of this piece’s narrative is a man “not fully aware of what he’s looking for … that ‘getting lost’ feeling is part of the character of this piece, which is so unique.” In all its tumult and frigidity, the piece offers listeners the freedom to get lost along the way, to leave their journeys open-ended or to go on wandering. articles.text: Noir City — the world’s largest annual film noir festival, now in its 22nd year — is in full swing at the Grand Lake Theatre every day through this Sunday, February 2. The theme for this year’s festival, hosted by Film Noir Foundation founder and Turner Classic Movies (TCM) host Eddie Muller, features 24 movies in 10 days and nights, shining a spotlight on women whose cinematic legacy is entwined with the rise of film noir. Many of this year’s films star the six actresses profiled in Muller’s 2002 book Dark City Dames: The Wicked Women of Film Noir, which is being reissued through a TCM book series in April 2025, in a newly revised and expanded edition. Jane Greer, Marie Windsor, Audrey Totter, Evelyn Keyes, Coleen Gray and Ann Savage are the core cadre of women featured in this year’s Noir City program, which includes many of their signature films, including, respectively, Out of the Past (1947), The Narrow Margin (1952), Tension (1949), The Prowler (1951), The Killing (1956) and Detour (1945). In addition to those acclaimed favorites, the program also highlights films starring nine other actresses notable for their performances in crime films of the era: Joan Bennett, Peggie Castle, Rhonda Fleming, Marsha Hunt, Ella Raines, Ruth Roman, Jan Sterling, Claire Trevor and Helen Walker. Not coincidentally, the expanded edition of Muller’s book includes new profiles of these women. “One thing I’ve learned after doing programs for 25 years,” Muller said, “is that you need to circle back and re-show the classics – the bedrock of the genre. Some of these films are wellknown to the hardcore, but for younger fans, who may have been in grade school when I started doing festivals, this will be the first time they’ve seen many of these movies … and certainly the first time on a big screen with an enthusiastic audience.” Muller noted that extra effort was made this year to secure as many 35mm prints as possible: “It’s harder than ever to show film prints, so it feels sort of Billy Wilder’s 1951 film Ace in the Hole, featuring Jan Sterling and Kirk Douglas, is just one of the many double-featured films running through this Sunday for this year’s femme fatale-themed Noir City festival at Grand Lake Theatre. valedictory.” Fourteen of the festival’s 24 offerings are film prints. “It’s remarkable to realize that when I began these festivals, everything was on film. No digital versions existed. Now, this might be the first — and last — time that younger viewers will see a 35mm film print, ”Miller added. “I’m very enthused about this year’s program because I had friendships with many of the women we’re celebrating and I’ll have plenty of stories to share — as well as being able to see these women again in all their glamorous glory,” Muller said. One sample of the double feature programs in the festival’s remaining week includes: Sunday, February 2 • The Prowler (Joseph Losey, 1951), 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Losey’s greatest American film, from a script by legendary screenwriter Dalton Trumbo, has a cop (Van Heflin) stalking a lonely, affluent housewife (Evelyn Keyes) and deciding to win her in time-honored noir tradition: by knocking off her husband. Don’t miss this opportunity to see one of the rarest — and most unusual—of all films noir in its original 35mm glory. • Ace in the Hole (Billy Wilder, 1951), 4 p.m. and 9 p.m. On its release, critics called this the most bitter, cynical and mean-spirited movie ever made. It still may hold the honor. What’s certain is how frighteningly prescient Wilder’s tale of mainstream media manipulation turned out to be. Kirk Douglas is stupendously rotten as a disgraced reporter reclaiming the spotlight by prolonging the plight of a trapped miner. A genuine masterpiece. Presented digitally. A full list of film schedules and tickets ($22.80 for a double feature) for the festival at Grand Lake Theatre (3200 Grand Avenue, Oakland) is available at noircity.com.

Italian-American pianist Cristiana Pegoraro is in our area for a series of concerts. Usually, touring musical artists are in town for a concert and then leave the next day. It is a fascinating experience, I assure The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet you. Her first warm-up piece was Robert Schumann’s Traumerei, which was truly dreamy as the name implies. Walkers explore results of Beautification projects Linda and Kingston Avenue in 1910 By Dick Carter It was another great mid-winter day last Wednesday when the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group met at the Exedra for their weekly walk, but there was a special reason to be there on this lovely morning. The Piedmont Beautification Foundation is celebrating 60 years of supporting projects that have made Piedmont even more beautiful. The Wednesday walkers were going to see sets of them this week and the following two weeks and recognize PBF’s contributions to Piedmont. The different projects that PBF has been a part of is impressive and can be seen at https://piedmontbeautificationfoundation. org. Current PBF President Patty Dunlap and past Park Commission Chair Patty Siskind were on hand as was Piedmont’s new KCOM Station Manager Jeff Shaw. The City of Piedmont wants to publicize PBF’s great work, so Jeff’s video team was going to tape the walk at the project sites. Patty Dunlap briefly told the walkers about PBF. It has been working since 1964, in partnership with the City of Piedmont, to create beautiful public spaces in Piedmont that build a strong sense of pride and community. The inspiration for PBF came from the Piedmont Garden Club, which continues to nominate the PBF officers. They are joined by the Piedmont mayor, vicemayor, and the chair of the Park Commission to provide advice on projects. Matt Gerhart had created three route maps to show the walkers this week and the next two. At each location, a PBF volunteer would be there to tell the walkers about the project. The first destination was the Jerome Triangle where Jerome and Fairview Avenues meet just below Oakland Avenue. The group went on Jerome in a long line to the triangle. The film crew was waiting for them and so was Public Works Supervisor Nick Millosovich, who described the creation of the triangle. The hazardous condition at the interseection of Jerome and Magnolia was first identified by nearby resident Ralph Marinelly. As a tribute to his efforts, the triangle and landscaping were dedicated to him. Nick told the walkers how the project to create the triangle started 37 years ago in 1988 and was completed in 1990. Eight 10-to-12-foot-tall redwoods in 24” boxes were planted and have grown into the large trees in the triangle today. Azaleas and rhododendrons were also planted, but the redwoods have a way of sucking moisture and nutrients from the soil that minimizes other trees and plants. Nick also said that redwoods’ shallow roots grow together tightly and make the ground around them hard. Redwoods should be in groves of at least three trees. They support each other and this reduces the risk of their being blown over in windstorms. Then it was off to their second PBF destination, the Linda/ Kingston Triangle. The group went down Oakland Avenue and after two cycles of traffic signals crossed Grand Avenue. They went up Howard Avenue, down Lake Avenue past Beach School, and up Linda Avenue to the triangle at Kingston Avenue. Jeff Shaw’s video crew was there to meet them. At the triangle Patty Siskind told the group how this community-suggested intersection improvement was created. Neighbors were concerned about children’s safety at this corner and pushed for the project. It took from 2014 to 2017 to complete, and PBF dedicated funds in 2016 for it. The north edge of the triangle is in Oakland and the project was coordinated with the City of Oakland. City of Piedmont Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent did the landscaping, and a bio-swale was incorporated to collect and percolate ground water. A handsome stone wall surrounds the triangle with two stone benches built into it and two bronze signs. One has the triangle’s name and history while the other proclaims, “Mom’s A Mensch. She Deserves A Bench. The Siskind Family.” Patty’s family members were rightly proud of her Park Commission work on this wonderful project. The long walk to the triangle and the city’s border had taken longer than was anticipated in Matt Gerhart’s route, so the walkers made their way back to the Exedra by a shorter route up Linda, Grand, Wildwood, and Magnolia Avenues. They enjoyed seeing these two PBF projects, appreciated Patty Dunlop, Patty Siskind, Jeff Shaw, Nick Millosovich, and Matt Gerhadt’s participation, and were looking forward to seeing more of PBF’s generous contributions to Piedmont in the next two weeks. The wine opens with a perfumed nose of honeysuckle and jasmine with pear and apple notes along with a hint of forest floor. This delightful wine is one of the best Chardonnays we have had in years. • 2022 Hartford Family Pinot Noir Fog Dance Vineyard, $78 This wine stood out in the flight of three Pinots. Would make a great partner to grilled salmon.

articles.text: It was the kind of day that demanded the top down on the convertible. One of those clear sky, crisp, perfect temperature winter days that reveal the incredible beauty of Sonoma County. We cruised the back roads outside of Healdsburg and turned off Martinelli Rd. onto the narrow winding path up to Hartford Family Winery. It was evident upon seeing the winery that great care had been taken in its planning. It is a beautifully proportioned classically styled building nestled in a small amphitheater of vines with an installation of solar panels showing the respect for the environment. We were escorted to a flagstone patio covered by a vine trellis that overlooked the vines. The Hartford Family winery was founded in 1994 by Don and Jennifer Hartford. They located their winery in the town of Forestville about 15 miles from the cool Pacific Coast. The Hartford Family Winery specializes in making wines from single vineyard sites believing small and low-yielding vineyards deliver expressive and personality-rich wines. “High risk, High reward” is their philosophy. In addition to their single vineyard wines, they have bottlings of Russian River Chardonnay, Pinot and Zinfandel that are made in larger quantities and are widely distributed across the US. Pete Wilkie, a trained sommelier, was our knowledgeable host as we tasted through the Hartford portfolio. The following wines were the highlight and are available through their website. • 2022 Hartford Family Chardonnay Far Coast Vineyard, $70 To be honest we are kind of over Chardonnay - nearly members of the ABC (Anything But Chardonnay) club. So, expectations were not high as Pete started the tasting with a flight of three single vineyard Chardonnays. Mauritson Winery in Healdsburg.

articles.text: On Friday, January 17, a group of the Piedmont Seniors ventured on a day’s outing to visit two of the East Bay’s most historic sites – the Berkeley City Club and the Claremont Club & Spa. The Berkeley City Club, a historical landmark organized in 1927, was one of the area’s earliest attempts by women to contribute to social, civic and cultural progress. The building, constructed in 1929, is one of the outstanding works of noted California architect Julia Morgan, whose successful interpretation of Moorish and Gothic elements in this monumental 6-story structure created a major landmark of California design. Julia Morgan, who grew up in Oakland, is perhaps best known as the architect of Hearst Castle at San Simeon, and the post-1906 earthquake rebuilding of San Francisco’s Fairmont Hotel. Morgan was also the architect of several houses in Piedmont. When the Piedmont Seniors arrived at Berkeley City Club, they were divided into two groups, each with a docent to guide them through the property. In the 1920s, women across the country were enjoying a new sense of civic involvement and educational interest. The women’s club movement offered educational, civic, recreational, and philanthropic opportunities. This “little castle” with its grand ballrooms, dining room, a variety of meeting rooms, residence rooms, and a beautiful swimming pool was just what the founding group had envisioned. Since 1962 this club has welcomed men and women alike, and in 1965 the name was changed from the Berkeley Women’s City Club to the Berkeley City Club. Today, along with its social club activities, the Berkeley City Club provides an elegant location for weddings, reunions, conferences, and meetings of civic groups. Once the tour was concluded the group met in the Club’s dining room for an elegant lunch. The restaurant renamed Julia’s, is open for lunch, dinner and weekly high teas. Visiting the Berkeley City Club’s historic swimming pool are docent Karen Yencich (left), Elene Manolis, Loretta Vanderveen, Janet Epstein, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Sue Getreuer, and Lilly Guardia-LaBar. Christensen, who gave the group a 45-minute tour of the many rooms of the main floor of the hotel, including those not open to the public. It is an historic American hotel that is situated at the foot of Claremont Canyon in the Berkeley Hills. It has 279 guest rooms, a 20,000-square-foot spa, 10 tennis courts, and 22 acres of landscaped gardens. It is situated on the Oakland/Berkeley border and is a designated Historical Landmark and a member of Historic Hotels of America. The site was developed initially by early settler William Butler Thornburgh, who constructed a large home on the site in 1870, which he called a “castle”. After a wildfire in the hills, the house burned to the ground, and on November 10, 1905, the property was acquired by Louis Titus on behalf of the Claremont Hotel Company for approximately $37,500. The Claremont Hotel Company was a group of investors that included, among others, Frank C. Havens of Piedmont. Construction was temporarily halted due to the 1906 earthquake, but resumed in 1910, and was completed in 1914. It finally opened in 1915 as the Claremont Hotel. The Claremont faced destruction in the 1991 Oakland firestorm, but firefighters and the lessening winds stopped the flames short of the hotel. In 2007 the Claremont was acquired by Morgan Stanley, but the resort filed for bankruptcy due to losses attributed to the ongoing recession. In 2014 it was purchased by the Fairmont Hotel chain and financier Richard Blum. Finally, in May 2023, the hotel was. Purchased by Ohana Real Estate Investors for $163 million. Overall, the Piedmont Seniors had a wonderful day going back in time. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area.

articles.text: Piedmont Seniors enjoy a festive holiday luncheon at the Claremont Country Club on December 13. On Friday, December 13 the Piedmont Seniors held their annual Holiday luncheon at the Claremont Country Club. The Club was all decked out in holiday decorations with white reindeers, ornaments, and tall Christmas trees throughout the facility. Originally founded as Oakland Golf Club, it was located by Lake Merritt in the Adams Point area of Oakland. In 1904 it relocated to its present site. Early in 1927 tragedy struck the thriving Claremont Country Club when a four-alarm fire completely destroyed the clubhouse. Two years later it was rebuilt largely to its present shape. The Seniors enjoyed a delicious three-course luncheon consisting of butternut squash bisque, and a choice of cordon bleu chicken breast or spinach and mushroom crepes, vanilla ice cream with chocolate sauce and a homemade cookie. There was a delightful pianist in attendance, who played holiday tunes in the Garden Room of the Club. Forty-three members and guests celebrated this event. There was a special tribute to Flo Bryan, who celebrated her 100th birthday with the group. After the meal the group exchanged gifts which is always a highlight at the party. The event put people in the holiday spirit and was most enjoyable for all. For more information about the Piedmont Seniors, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors’ group has monthly meetings on the 4th Wednesday of each month at 10 am at the Piedmont Community Hall. They also go on monthly excursions to diverse locations throughout the Bay Area. Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein presents a poinsettia plant to celebrate Flo Bryan’s 100th birthday.

articles.text: Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama, I am trying to get my estate in order so I can update my trust. One of my friends recommended I keep myself organized on my computer. I have no idea how to even get started. My attorney wants my updated beneficiary list and changes. How do I begin? Lissa R., Oakland Dear Lissa, When you realize how valuable a tool a computer can be to get yourself organized for things like managing your beneficiary list for your trust and will, managing your medical expenses, etc., it helps with the stress of getting ready for the inevitable. Since I am assuming you don’t plan to try to create your will and trust by yourself without an attorney, here are some ways to get organized. 1. Create a folder for all of the documents you need. You might label it Trust and Will 2025. In this folder, you can keep scanned documents to help you get organized: bank account, account numbers, and any documents that you create. 2. Get your documents in order It’s very likely that your financial planner or stockbroker has a guide how to organize your documents to make it easier for your executor or family members to proceed in the event of your death. You should organize things like investment accounts, bank, accounts, and assets. If you are making a trust for the first time, you should know the limits of what you can have before things go to probate. If you have a lot of money in your checking account, for example, you should make sure it doesn’t exceed the limit to necessitate probate. Assets are subject to probate if they are not in trust, jointly held, or if a beneficiary designation is not in place. As a reference, decedent estates had to be probated when assets subject to probate exceeded $184,500 for persons who passed away in 2023. And assets aggregate maximum value threshold for 2023 was $25,000. Each item’s value cannot exceed $5000. So if you have artwork worth more than $5000 apiece, you want to make sure that is put in the trust. Again, it’s important to talk to your financial advisor about the state of your accounts. You can keep copies of investment statements, bank statements, etc. in your organizational folder. 3. Create a spreadsheet Your Mac comes with spreadsheet, word processor, and presentation software. The spreadsheet software is called Numbers. Of course, many of us have Microsoft products, and that case you can use Excel if you have that on your computer. Then you can make headings for the types of beneficiaries that you may have. The headings can be family, friends, and nonprofits and charities. For the nonprofits and charities, you will need their addresses, their EIN numbers phone numbers and or email. If you’re not even sure which charities to choose, you can use a well-known site like charitynavigator.org. This very useful site gives you ratings for the charities, as well as all of their contact and Tax ID information.

articles.text: Widely respected plastic surgeon who created large floats for Piedmont 4th of July Parade It is with profound sadness that we announce the passing of our beloved husband, father, and grandfather, Dr. Ronald P. Gruber, who left this world peacefully on Saturday January 18th, surrounded by his loving family. Born on April 13, 1941, in London, England to parents fleeing the holocaust, his family emigrated to the U.S. when he was five. Following the family’s early years in New York, they moved to Oakland. Ron graduated from Oakland High School in 1958, UC Berkeley in 1962, and UCSF School of Medicine in 1966. He began surgical training at Montefiore in New York but was interrupted to serve as a Captain in the U.S. Army where he did research in wound ballistics and learned to fly planes. Returning to California, he completed his plastic surgery training at Stanford University. In 1975 Ron returned to the East Bay, settled in Piedmont, and opened his plastic surgery practice in Oakland. He worked tirelessly to become a world-renowned rhinoplasty surgeon and was considered a leading authority in the field. Although his practice was based in the Bay Area, patients from all over the world traveled to be in his care. Ron understood that “successful results are the product of years of training, skill, compassion, honesty, and the blending of two disciplines – science and artistry.” Selfless and tireless, he gave back to the plastic surgery community and rhinoplasty in particular. Author of Rhinoplasty State of the Art and over 100 articles on the subject, he explained to the novice rhinoplasty surgeon basic and advanced techniques to provide superior results. He was generous with sharing his knowledge as Adjunct Professor of Plastic Surgery at Stanford and at UCSF. Ron was a founding member and President of the Rhinoplasty Society. In his zeal to improve and invent, Ron designed and created The Gruber Rhinoplasty Set – a surgical instrument set being used by many surgeons today. But this was just a footnote in Ron’s amazing life. Ron was a polymath. He had a passion for so many things and excelled not only in medicine, but the sciences and the arts. He undertook any new subject and dissected it cleanly until he fully understood where he could make a difference. Ron was fascinated by the aspect of the time continuum. With Albert Einstein as his inspiration, he delved into the elasticity of time and was published in the field of Astrophysics. If you were fortunate enough to attend one of his lectures about Relativity you would walk away with a good basic understanding of an incredibly complex topic. He probed into the relationship of physics and psychology, authoring 16 articles on the subject, and a book, Time is an Illusion. He co-chaired a symposium at Stanford on the Nature of Time. His latest experimental venture was using virtual reality to resolve the dilemma of this illusion. Ron’s contributions extended beyond his career and family. He was an active member of his community, often lending his time and expertise to charitable and community causes. Starring principal dancer Nikisha Fogo, the first Black principal dancer in the history of the San Francisco Ballet, Chroma has been described as a groundbreaking ballet, “a shock to the system,” merging cutting-edge choreography with a rhythmically complex, rock-inspired score. Fogo had already captivated audiences during the Company’s production of The Nutcracker this past Christmas season; In Chroma, she stepped into the role previously performed by the iconic Yuan Yuan Tan for the San Francisco Ballet. Fogo’s interpretation was both powerful and precise, which was no small feat given the ballet’s demanding choreography. The evening concluded with the finale from Symphony in C. Choreographed by George Balanchine to Bizet’s score, the piece dazzled with its scale and energy, featuring 50 dancers—a near-complete showcase of the entire troupe. For those pining for the elegance of tutus amidst the contemporary costumes of the night, this performance delivered. Balanchine’s bold interpretation of the classical technique shone through, creating a sense of unity and spectacle. With its scale and majesty, the Gala’s closing number evoked the grandeur of Swan Lake, albeit with a more jubilant tone. The perfect finale, it was met with a thunderous ovation. The beauty of the Gala is that when the curtain falls, the celebration doesn’t stop. All it takes is a short walk across Van Ness to continue the festivities at City Hall. (Of course, you’ll need an after-party ticket, but at $175 each, it’s a solid deal given the amenities: several open bars, multiple food stations offering everything from sushi and dim sum to charcuterie and desserts, and three dance stages, some illuminated for added flair.) There’s no better place to flaunt a gown than on City Hall’s grand staircase—long, broad, and offering a perfect vantage point of the foyer and central stage. At times, it felt like you were stepping into a movie or a Broadway show with Vegas lights, and yet, you don’t feel like an outsider. That’s the magic of art: as long as you’re a fellow traveler, you belong. There was plenty of dancing, live music and singing to the likes of “Sweet Dreams.” While the DJ’s choices may have at times felt conventional, as lamented by one of the party’s more eccentric attendees, for those on the dance floor, myself included, they proved riveting enough. Given that the festivities, which began at 10 pm, extended into the early morning hours, a lounge was thoughtfully arranged in the South Light Court. Here, on plush blue velvet couches, guests could converse with friends – — assuming they had the foresight to attend—or simply observe the lively scene while enjoying a cocktail or two (or perhaps three or four—nobody was counting). Throughout the night, boredom was conspicuously absent, and unsurprisingly, no one departed early. As I made my way to my car, I found myself already anticipating the 2026 Gala. The greatest part, of course, is that San Francisco Ballet’s season has just begun. Over the next few months, all you need to do is cross the Bay Bridge to the Civic Center (BART is another option, with walking groups to the theater before and after shows). From the Gala, it’s clear that Tamara Rojo’s new season will be an exciting one, featuring both classical and contemporary, genre-bending works, while showcasing plenty of talent. You can buy individual and season tickets at sfballet. org. I’ll certainly be returning to experience the pieces glimpsed at the Gala in their full glory, and I hope to see you there. And don’t forget to mark January 24, 2026, the night of the opening gala, on your social calendar. After all, it is the best party in town. Rodrigo wrote that the concerto captures “the fragrance of magnolias, the singing of birds, and the gushing of fountains.” The piece has been performed and recorded numerous times in many forms since its premiere in 1940 — including as part of Miles Davis’s Sketches of Spain and by jazz pianist Chick Corea as part of his composition Spain. California Symphony’s featured guitar soloist, Meng Su, has performed in over 30 countries and is on the faculty at the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. Classical Guitar Magazine reports that she has the “star potential to serve as inspiration for new generations of guitarists to come.” Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s Symphony No. 41 in C Major is his final symphony, and his longest and grandest. The work is commonly known as the Jupiter Symphony, named after the Roman god for its grand scale. Mozart completed the monumental piece in a brief two-month period over the summer of 1788, along with his Symphonies Nos. 39 and 40, creating a final trilogy of works that has puzzled scholars: it’s unknown for what occasion he wrote them, since they were not commissioned by any patron for any specific performance, an anomaly in Mozart’s career. A majestic, intricate, exuberant masterpiece, Mozart’s Symphony No. 41, his final symphony, is one of his most celebrated and frequently performed works, showcasing a genius at the height of his powers. “In choosing music to precede a great milestone such as Mozart’s final symphony, I decided that it was best to showcase music of a completely different and opposing style and aesthetic,” California Symphony Artistic and Music Director Donato Cabrera said. “Simon’s Breathe is contemplative and meditative music that speaks softly but carries a big stick,” he continued. “It has a natural forthrightness to it that is beguiling and gently invites one to just be present in the moment.
